newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian nukes are reliable, defence minister says.
newsitem.headline: Russian nukes are reliable, defence minister says.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Rodionov assured President Boris Yeltsin on Monday that the command and control system governing Russia's nuclear missiles was reliable, the Kremlin said.

Rodionov's comments at a one-hour meeting in the Kremlin appeared to reverse remarks last month in which he expressed concern that underfunding of the armed forces raised doubts about the reliabilty of Russia's nuclear weapons.

"As the defence minister underlined in his report, the system controlling the country's strategic nuclear forces answers all demands, is reliable and stable, which excludes the possibility of unusual situations," the presidential press service said in a written statement.
The statement also quoted Rodionov as saying: "The morale and psychological training of the personal staff who are on military duty...is at a high level."
The statement followed a weekend article in a popular newspaper suggesting Russia could accidentally launch a nuclear missile attack because its systems were unreliable.

The Kremlin gave no sign that Yeltsin was about to dismiss his 60-year-old defence minister in a government reshuffle which he has been working on with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and first deputy prime minister Anatoly Chubais.
Rodionov has been demanding higher defence spending to reform the armed forces, saying he is in charge of a "disintegrating army and a dying navy".
He told Russian media chiefs on February 7 that Russia could soon "reach the threshold beyond which its rockets and nuclear systems cannot be controlled".
Yeltsin publicly scolded him last month, telling him to stop "whingeing" and get on with reforms.
The presidential press service said Yeltsin and Rodionov had also discussed plans for Russia's nuclear arms for the years 2006 to 2008.

This included discussion of the prospects for negotiating a START-3 treaty to follow the START-2 treaty with the United States which is to cut strategic nuclear warheads to a limit of 3,500 each. The Russian parliament has yet to ratify START-2.

"B. Yeltsin allows the possibliity of further cuts in the strategic nuclear forces to reasonable levels under equal obligations on the Russian and American sides and, of course, not violating Russia's national interests," the statement said.

Washington has proposed new reductions to 2,000 to 2,500 warheads per side and wants Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton to agree at a summit in Helsinki this week to a start in negotiations on START-3 as soon as START-2 is ratified.
Yeltsin indicated in a television interview on Monday that there would be no START-3 treaty until differences over the interpretation of the 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile (ABM) treaty are resolved.
Parliament has not ratified START-2 partly because it fears Washington could develop a national ballistic missile defence system which it says could violate the ABM treaty.
